{{Essay-like|date=May 2023}}

The deaf/Deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) population is underrepresented in science, technology, engineering, and math fields (STEM), despite a history of excellence in these fields. The lack of standard American Sign Language (ASL) vocabulary, engaging hands-on learning environments, and DHH mentors seems to contribute largely to the discrepancy.

== History ==
DHH scientists, inventors, engineers, and mathematicians have contributed greatly to the world. The field of astronomy, in particular, has been blessed with many DHH scholars who have immensely advanced the field, including [[Robert Grant Aitken|Robert Aitken]], [[Annie Jump Cannon]], [[John Goodricke]], [[Olaf Hassel]], and [[Henrietta Swan Leavitt]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=G. |first=Lang, Harry |url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/31374052 |title=Deaf persons in the arts and sciences : a biographical dictionary |date=1995 |publisher=Greenwood Press |isbn=0-313-29170-5 |oclc=31374052}}</ref> [[Konstantin Tsiolkovsky]] was one of the founding fathers of astronautics and rocketry. In addition, the [[Gallaudet Eleven]] were Deaf research subjects in the 1950s and 1960s, essential for [[NASA]]'s study of the effects of weightlessness on humans.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Almeida |first=Andres |date=2017-05-02 |title=How 11 Deaf Men Helped Shape NASA's Human Spaceflight Program |url=http://www.nasa.gov/feature/how-11-deaf-men-helped-shape-nasas-human-spaceflight-program |access-date=2023-04-19 |website=NASA}}</ref>

== DHH statistics in STEM ==
The DHH population in the U.S. has fewer associate's and bachelor's degrees than their hearing peers (27.7% vs. 43.3% for associate degrees, 18.8% vs. 34% for bachelor's degrees), and this gap has persisted for the last decade across ages, genders, and races. The difference seems due to lower rates of entry into associate's and bachelor's programs, since DHH students complete their bachelor's degrees at rates similar to their hearing peers.<ref name=":0">{{Cite report |last1=Garberoglio |first1=Carrie Lou |last2=Palmer |first2=Jeffrey Levi |last3=Cawthon |first3=Stephanie W. |last4=Sales |first4=Adam |date=2019 |publisher=The University Of Texas At Austin |title=Deaf People and Educational Attainment in the United States: 2019 |url=https://repositories.lib.utexas.edu/handle/2152/83051 |language=en |doi=10.26153/TSW/10052}}</ref> From 2001 through 2010, only 0.17% of the doctorate degrees given in the U.S. were to DHH students.<ref>National Science Foundation, Division of Science Resources Statistics. 2011. Women, Minorities, and Persons with Disabilities in Science and Engineering: 2011. Special Report NSF 11-309. Arlington, VA. Available at [http://www.nsf.gov/statistics/wmpd/].</ref> This number increased to 1.2% by 2014.<ref>National Science Foundation, Division of Science Resources Statistics. 2015. Women, Minorities, and Persons with Disabilities in Science and Engineering: 2015. Special Report NSF 15-311. Arlington, VA. Available at [http://www.nsf.gov/statistics/wmpd/].</ref>  Employment rates for DHH graduates also lag behind their hearing peers, particularly in science and engineering fields.<ref name=":0" /> Approximately 2.8% of scientists and engineers employed in the U.S. in 2019 reported having a moderate or severe hearing disability.<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Survey of College Graduates: 2019 {{!}} NSF - National Science Foundation |url=https://ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsf22310 |access-date=2023-04-19 |website=ncses.nsf.gov}}</ref>

== ASL STEM vocabulary ==
One obstacle for the DHH population is the limited standard ASL vocabulary of STEM concepts. Because these signs develop in different locations, many different signs are often given for the same word or concept. For example, the sign for "protein" has at least five different signs in the various databases listed below. This makes both communication and education in their native language difficult for the DHH population in STEM fields.

Efforts headed by [[Harry G. Lang]] began in the 1970s to catalog STEM signs for use in education through the NTID Technical Signs Project, which became the NTID Science Signs Lexicon.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NTID Science Signs Lexicon: A Brief History for Those Developing Newer Resources - Science Signs Lexicon - RIT Wiki |url=https://wiki.rit.edu/display/sciencelexicon/ |access-date=2023-04-19 |website=wiki.rit.edu}}</ref> The database is no longer accessible to the public, but NTID has since established both ASLCORE<ref>{{Cite web |title=Home {{!}} ASLCORE |url=http://aslcore.org/ |access-date=2023-04-19 |website=aslcore.org}}</ref> and the DeafTEC STEM dictionary.<ref>{{Cite web |title=STEM Dictionary – STEM Dictionary |url=https://deaftec.org/stem-dictionary/ |access-date=2023-04-19 |website=deaftec.org}}</ref> Several other databases have also emerged, including ASL CLeaR,<ref>{{Cite web |title=ASL Clear |url=https://www.aslclear.org/ |access-date=2023-04-19 |website=www.aslclear.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Reis |first1=Jeanne |last2=Solovey |first2=Erin T. |last3=Henner |first3=Jon |last4=Johnson |first4=Kathleen |last5=Hoffmeister |first5=Robert |title=Proceedings of the 17th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers & Accessibility - ASSETS '15 |chapter=ASL CLeaR |date=2015 |chapter-url=http://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?doid=2700648.2811343 |language=en |location=Lisbon, Portugal |publisher=ACM Press |pages=441–442 |doi=10.1145/2700648.2811343 |isbn=978-1-4503-3400-6|s2cid=32298961 }}</ref> the ASL STEM Forum,<ref>{{Cite web |title=ASL STEM |url=https://aslstem.web.app/ |access-date=2023-04-19 |website=aslstem.web.app |language=en}}</ref> and the TERC Signing Math and Science Dictionaries.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Signing Math and Science |url=https://signsci.terc.edu/ |access-date=2023-04-19 |website=signsci.terc.edu}}</ref> The Atomic Hands website<ref>{{Cite web |title=Atomic Hands |url=https://atomichands.com/ |access-date=2023-04-19 |language=en-US}}</ref> acts as a clearinghouse for these databases and for ASL STEM curriculum, in addition to producing their own ASL STEM videos and a networking database for Deaf STEM professionals.

Previous research on ASL STEM vocabulary determined standard signs were more likely to be used by teachers in science classes if they accurately depicted scientific concepts, but invented signs showed no patterns of preference.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lang |first1=H. G. |last2=Hupper |first2=M. L. |last3=Monte |first3=D. A. |last4=Brown |first4=S. W. |last5=Babb |first5=I. |last6=Scheifele |first6=P. M. |date=2006-08-17 |title=A Study of Technical Signs in Science: Implications for Lexical Database Development |url=https://academic.oup.com/jdsde/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/deafed/enl018 |journal=Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=65–79 |doi=10.1093/deafed/enl018 |pmid=16952932 |issn=1081-4159|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== DHH STEM education ==
Many studies have suggested that hands-on, inquiry-based learning is ideal for DHH students since traditional teaching methods rely heavily on lectures and printed materials such as textbooks, which may be more difficult to process for DHH students who are native signers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wang |first=Ye |date=2011 |title=Inquiry-Based Science Instruction and Performance Literacy for Students Who Are Deaf or Hard of Hearing |url=http://muse.jhu.edu/content/crossref/journals/american_annals_of_the_deaf/v156/156.3.wang.html |journal=American Annals of the Deaf |language=en |volume=156 |issue=3 |pages=239–254 |doi=10.1353/aad.2011.0031 |pmid=21941875 |s2cid=41742089 |issn=1543-0375}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McIntosh |first1=R. Anne |last2=Sulzen |first2=Lynn |last3=Reeder |first3=Kate |last4=Kidd |first4=Dawn Holt |date=1994 |title=Making Science Accessible to Deaf Students: The Need for Science Literacy and Conceptual Teaching |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/18/article/542002 |journal=American Annals of the Deaf |volume=139 |issue=5 |pages=480–484 |doi=10.1353/aad.1994.0007 |pmid=7856496 |s2cid=27128540 |issn=1543-0375}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gormally |first=Cara |date=2017-03-01 |title=Deaf, Hard-of-Hearing, and Hearing Signing Undergraduates' Attitudes toward Science in Inquiry-Based Biology Laboratory Classes |journal=CBE: Life Sciences Education |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=ar6 |doi=10.1187/cbe.16-06-0194 |pmc=5332049 |pmid=28188279}}</ref>

A 2018 study with Gallaudet STEM majors found that Deaf students had better undergraduate research experiences with hearing mentors when they educated their colleagues about Deaf culture, strongly advocated for themselves, had mentors that were willing to work closely with them, and worked with other Deaf students.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Majocha |first1=Megan |last2=Davenport |first2=Zachary |last3=Braun |first3=Derek C. |last4=Gormally |first4=Cara |date=2018 |title="Everyone Was Nice...But I Was Still Left Out": An Interview Study About Deaf Interns' Research Experiences in STEM |journal=Journal of Microbiology & Biology Education |language=en |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=19.1.10 |doi=10.1128/jmbe.v19i1.1381  |doi-access=free|issn=1935-7877 |pmc=5969436 |pmid=29904550}}</ref>
